title: What's the most frustrating combat UI design elements?

posts.author: hyunko
posts.body:
When it comes to traditional JRPGs, be it RPGmaker games or other engines (such as Octopath, Persona5, older FF games, etc), what is the most frustrating part of combat menus and combat UI?
I always felt like the turn-based combat is a very fine tightrope, where it's either a massive strength or a massive weakness and I have noticed that aside from music and visuals, it's often menus that frustrate me.
Be it slow scrolling, not seeing a lot of spells at a time or an annoying SFX with every scroll.
What's your most hated aspects of combat menus and UI?

posts.author: TRIDIUM

posts.author: SundialShark
posts.body:
I hate it when skill/combat UI doesn't tell me too much of anything when selecting skills besides flavor text OR I have to spend too much time thinking of what the skill is even supposed to do (and if there are multiple costs, I don't want to spend too much time thinking about which resource it's going to drain out from). Here, I define the skill name but also the type/scope it is also very clear. Costs are clear. I can even kinda see what's going on behind the scenes as I select my next move. Stuff like this is super important to me. I'm not perfect, but I threw in a scroll bar too if there's a lot to go through. I could have doubled the number of columns but I still wanted to see the active battle keep going.
TL;DR: Don't make me read a book in your Help window, but don't be too brief either.

You and me are on the same page here, actually. But let me add on with:
Spoiler:
This frustrating aspect of the Help Window in combat
The gap between the help window and the skill window is very annoying, because it doesn't help your eyes properly settle on where you should be looking + at worst, the information at the top doesn't register that it belongs to the skill you're currently selecting.
Likewise, big agree on the actual skill description either being overwritten or useless because it's all flavor text that doesn't actually tell you what it does. I see people putting actual damage formulas or static "expected damage" into their skill descriptions and it's pretty ugly every time.
Spoiler:
Here's what I did to fix it
As well as extending the help window so it's three lines instead of just two.
* You can see if the attack does Physical/Magical damage or if it's a support move (as indicated by a green dot or a pink heart for healing attacks).
* Speed priority, if it makes contact (for enemies with contact-activated abilities like thorns) and if it removes or adds status effects.
Also, tangentially related - I kinda hate RPG Maker's inventory system for combat. It just throws literally everything in there without any organization. So I had to split it up per-item:
(Kinda like how Pokemon handles its battle inventory post Gen-3, now that I think about it.)
--
As for my actual reply to
@hyunko
's original post:
Gonna give a +1 to everyone saying "annoying sound effects". Using the stock sound effects is also grating, since ideally you'd want the game to sound like it belongs to you. (And it gets really weird if you have a lot of custom art but little to no custom sound effects...)
That said, in my experience, the number one most frustrating combat UI design aspect is menu fatigue. It seems innocent at first having to manually scroll over to use different options, but the more party members you get and the more you have to keep selecting skills and confirming through different windows, the more it's like "I just want to hit the enemy already!"
For this purpose, I designed a system where pressing 1-9 on the keyboard allows you to instantly open a menu / shoot off an attack / guard, etc. regardless of where the cursor is. It streamlines the process to the point where I find it unplayable with it removed.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
My personal gripes with UI in games (not limited to RPG's or RPG Maker):
Too Busy Menu/HUD
There's just too much going on.  Too many colors, too much flash, too many icons, overloaded with information (necessary or extraneous, doesn't matter), too much art design on it.  I don't like visual overload.  I don't like having to discern what's important, visually, from what is not.  I don't like separating your art assets out from pertinent gameplay information.  It's overly stimulating in those cases.  Less is more.
Features that Blend Into The Environment
Most often, this is some menu design that makes the menu unclear if it's part of the background of the game or not.  Like it shares the same "through line" for colors used, patterns, or art style as assets in the game world.
However, this also moves into territory like "You pick up a note and it's written in cursive old english, so it's difficult to decipher!".  Stuff like this drives me crazy.  Yes, destroy my immersion by giving me something difficult to read.  Super helpful.
Anything that blends an aspect of your game into a "background element" tends to grind my gears.
The worst offenders of this that I see tend to be the "you can pick up an item in the environment" stuff.  Either it's not obvious it's something you can interact with... or what you use to make it obvious makes it harder to see as well (I have played at least half a dozen games where a sparkle effect was not spotted by me because the sparkle was the same freakin' color as what it was sitting on).
Annoying Menu Music
Ever since I played Dead Rising 4, I've not had a tolerance for this practice.  For context:  It's a zombie killing game with lots of over-the-top unbelieable stuff set shortly after "Black Friday".  When you open the pause menu... CHRISTMAS MUSIC!  In a setting or game with the theme of "Christmas", it might be welcome... but... this is not the place for it.  The game is very much a "Black Friday" game, and it references it constantly, and there's very little reference to Christmas at all... but that menu will drill Christmas music into your brain at every opportunity.
Since that game, I've paid more attention to menu music and whether or not it "grates on my nerves" or "fits the theme of the game very well".  I've noticed if it doesn't mesh well, it does actually impact my enjoyment of the game when it's for long stints of time (like anything beyond two hours, it will affect my enjoyment).
Information Overload
One of the main reasons I no longer engage in games like Final Fantasy Tactics anymore is because menus and character stat sheets are just so packed with information that it's impossible to parse it unless you're some sort of savant or you study it like it's a school test.  I've mostly given up on tactical maneuvering games as a result of this "stat overkill" stuff.  I don't want to look at a menu and see 8 main stats, 6 sub stats, 9 defensive/offensive stats (including accuracy, critical hit rate, critical hit defense, evasion, status inflict chance, status inflict evasion, etcetera), plus some religion or "faith" stat.  It's too much.  It's overkill.
I do not want to monitor more than a dozen stats.  Heck, I'd be happy if I only had to manage 8 total stats in most games (health, magic, magic attack, physical attack, defense, critical hit rate, evasion, chance to hit).
Like... for me, this is overkill:
I jacked the image from google, I don't own it, this isn't my character.  But look at this.  Modern stat sheets for the game have removed the elemental resistance stuff and just gave all jobs MP as far as I can tell, but there's still just an insane amount of stats to deal with there.
And, it's even worse because what does a Defense of "2391" even do?  What is the difference if Defense was 2400 instead?  Is there a difference?
What use is all this information to me, as a player?
Lack of Information
This is a personal gripe of mine.  A game that has a "health bar" for me or the enemy, but no numerical value tied to it.  How much HP total do I actually have?  Can I take 3 gunshots or 4?  Will the enemy die in 6 hits or 10?  I can see the bars visually go down, but it doesn't tell me much.  Did my attack do 92 damage or 93?  If the enemy has 186 health, but I'm doing 92 damage a hit... I gotta hit it 3 times.  But, the meter going down for 92 and 93 damage looks so similar!
Honestly, I prefer these meters just be gone if you're going to be vague about it.  If I'm never meant to know how much HP the enemy has, then just remove the meter to make the effect complete.  But, if I'm meant to see how much HP they have, then put a number on it so I can actually make intelligent combat choices with that information.
You're giving me Information Blue Marbles here.  Knock it off.
Now, this can apply to other stuff in the game, not just HP.  But, anything that is "vague" when it REALLY shouldn't be, is a problem.
"Raises Critical Hit Rate".  Okay, by how much?  5%?  Okay, 5% of what?  Does that mean I'll land a Critical Hit rate 5% more often?  Are some enemies resistant to critical hits and have defense to it?  Then what does that percentage actually mean?
I need more to work with.
Menu Fatigue
Too much scrolling, having to open the menu too much, having to access everything from the menu, having to fiddle with the menu for every little thing.
I expect menu interaction in most games.  But, once I begin approaching "I am spending 10% of my game time in a menu", I begin to get fatigue.  The higher that percentage goes, the worse it gets, until I just quit.

I can get why they do this in FF14. The stat tiering actively changes as you level. 2400 def at lv 70 is 36% passive mitigation, but at lv 90 the same 2400 def is 18%. all of the non-mainstats are like that.
There was a meme setup in eureka that capitalized on this before they changed eureka buffs like protect L to be flat % mits. A lv 60 tank (real level, not elemental level) in aug shire gear and the flat DEF bonus from Protect L used to hit 100% DR and become immune to all damage in eureka because the tiering difference between lv 60 and 70 causes the flat bonus to be worth much more than intended
I wish they would just say how much % your crit, defence, det/ten bonuses, etc. were, but in doing that, theyd be showing their jank ass stat system where the stat's effectiveness gets worse over time as you level without the stat value actually changing. People already know how they work, so we shouldnt have to break out the allagan studies spreadsheet, or set up a gear set on etro, or use the better stat sheet plugin on dalamud to know what our stat tiers are at.
Tai_MT said:
Like... for me, this is overkill:
Click to expand...
Worst part about it is that it looks like information overload at a glance, but at the same time, the way stats and gearing in the game is designed most of those stats are meaningless, redundant, or inconsistent too.
Main attributes are effectively tied to your average ilvl. Theres a linear formula as to how much each piece of gear gives you based on their ilvl. Unless you go out of your way to skew the average by doing something like wearing better armor and worse accs or wearing NQ crafted gear, theres going to be very little variance to what your main stats could even be at any given average ilvl. And even if you did that to skew your stats intentionally, it still wouldnt vary that much and ilvl syncs remove any function for it.
Even when element resists were actual stats and you could slot materia for them, all they really did was add a tremendously low chance to negate the damage of magic of that element. they did reduce damage from that element a tiny amount overall, but its real use was a back end during raid mechanics. element resistance and vulnerability buffs and debuffs did impact those stats, but they adjusted it by a massive degree compared to your ability to build for them that the answer was always "just do the mechanic" instead of  "sac all your materia slots to get overkilled by slightly less damage"
Then on SAM, both stats under role are useless. Neither TEN nor PIE affected dps roles at all back in SB (or even now).
The class has no magics of any kind and iaijutsu cast times scale with SKS, so everything under mental stats is pointless to display.
Every mainstat that isnt VIT or STR affects nothing in combat for non-ninja melee dps.
Non SAM specific points:
Attack power is just STR, unless youre on aiming or scouting, in which case its DEX. Thats fair
Attack magic potency is just INT, even on classes like NIN, DRK and PLD that have magics that dont use INT. Completely misleading as one could assume that you shouldn't use holy spirit and the confeteor combo on PLD, or mudras other than fuma on NIN at all based on the attack magic potency stat displayed. But despite them being magic damage theyre actually based on attack potency, which is their STR and DEX respectively for those classes... Then theres the exception being that if youre on a healer attack magic potency is MND. but...
Healing magic potency is just MND, even on classes like PLD and RDM that have healing spells that dont use MND. So on top of clemency and vercure *looking* like theyd be garbage heals based on the healing potency stat alone (especially since a SMN's physick IS garbage since it scales off of healing magic potency), for healers, both attack and healing magic potency will always the same number.
Even though they removed some of the stats in the character panel, alot of it is STILL irrelevant or redundant garbage today

One of the things that irritates me the most is getting stuck in the story or dealing with unnecessary linearity. For example, you're in the middle of a town and you need to fetch an egg and take it to the priest. posts.author: comradecid
posts.body:
having only just stumbled across this thread, i am immensely grateful for having found it, and for the insightful comments therein. i'm also relieved to discover that i'm not the only one in the world whose eyes glaze over when presented with a sea of arcane stats, and whose heart sinks upon discovering that a lack of complete mastery over those stats limits my ability to fully enjoy gameplay.
long ago, i embraced videogame rpgs, due partly to my experience with tabletop alternatives. i was intimidated by the complex practise of calculating arbitrary values employed in odd ways at seemingly random times, simultaneously feeling very alone and out-of-depth when all i wanted is to dive into a world that i could adapt to in my own way, and at my own pace.
even now, as a technically-capable and experienced adult (who still inexplicably loves rpgs), i have yet to see a game that clearly indicates what is important, what isn't, what means what (without having to look  up online in an outside wiki), and what effect things have at the end of the day on regular gameplay. over time, i've come to suspect that many of the common complaints regarding combat UI design (infuriatingly repetitive sounds, unnecessarily labourious interactions, impenetrable or vague contextual content, etc.) stem in part from those aforementioned deficiencies.
these problems are further fueled by well-intended-yet-clumsy efforts to enrich and deepen gameplay and the overall experience: 'juicing' interaction and effects to increase delight and a sense of 'weight', point inflation to imply greater effect or importance, ever-more stats to place more control over engine mechanics into the hands of the most zealous players, new aspects and features that demand ever-greater levels of expertise and effort, etc.
i am convinced that there might be a better approach to this. or at least, something less exhausting. i'm wondering if a simpler, more pragmatic system could be employed, that could still deliver engaging gameplay.
a few questions i'm keen to see answered:
- if you had to present an at-a-glance, bare-minimum set of stats to the player, which would allow them to quickly understand (even if only in broad strokes) their current status, and whether they might be able to survive the next encounter with an enemy... what stats would you show? what minimum information would the player need to make meaningful decisions?
- if stats such as INT, DEF, DEX, DEM, ABC, XYZ, etc. were indicated using indecipherable symbols instead of text/acronyms, how might a player come to understand each stat's role, utility, and potential in gameplay? could a player learn how to use this system without ever truly knowing the actual identity of its composite parts?
- if mana/magic points didn't exist, but the player could still use magic
that did not depend upon or draw from MP
... mechanically speaking, how could the player cast a spell whilst in combat? what would the player experience during gameplay? what restrictions might it entail, and what possibilities might it unlock?
- if experience points/levels didn't exist, how would you indicate/demonstrate to the player their 'progress' and level of personal development? what is 'experience'? if it played an active mechanical part of an overall system, what would that be?

You talk about "unlocking possibilities" like this is some sort of foreign system, but there are tons of games with it
Any game based on Dungeons & Dragons (which I'd assume you're familiar with, saying you come from tabletop gaming) uses a spell slot system, not anything to do with MP.
The entire Suikoden series uses items you place into slots to gain groups of skills, all of which have limited slot usage.
Phantasy Star 4 has both an MP system and skills that have limited usage.
There are also plenty of games that don't have point or slot restrictions, but just skill cooldowns.
comradecid said:
- if experience points/levels didn't exist, how would you indicate/demonstrate to the player their 'progress' and level of personal development?
Click to expand...
Again, many games have done this, where you don't have distinct character levels but gain levels or proficiency in specific skills as you use them, or gain skill points at specific times, etc. Or even don't
have
any kind of progression like that through the game, but just gain access to new skills or items at predetermined times.
The character level concept is just very prevalent because it's an easy and elegant way to monitor and control the player's progression for balance purposes.

It really wouldn't hurt you to summarize some of that and maybe tone down the flowery language a little.  It's a little "rough" to read as it doesn't flow very well and has a lot of "redundancy" in its presentation.
I'm the guy who gets ChatGP called on him for his excessively long and meandering posts.  So, if I am having some issues with the length/language of the post... well...
Anyway, I do have a question from this portion:
What is a "Tabletop Alternative", if you don't mean video games?  You say you embraced video games because of your "experience with previous tabletop alternatives".  I'm not really sure what you mean or what kinds of games you're talking about.  Card games?  Make Believe in the backyard with friends?
comradecid said:
- if you had to present an at-a-glance, bare-minimum set of stats to the player, which would allow them to quickly understand (even if only in broad strokes) their current status, and whether they might be able to survive the next encounter with an enemy... what stats would you show? what minimum information would the player need to make meaningful decisions?
Click to expand...
This is a sort of vague question.  It has several moving parts in it that simply don't mesh with the question you're asking.
To know if your character will "survive the next encounter with the enemy", you would need access to information you aren't addressing.
1.  Enemy stats including health.
2.  Damage formulas.
3.  Enemy tactics and skills.
4.  Player skill (or lack thereof).
After all, I could present you with basic stats of this:
Player
Attack: 15
Defense: 12
Health: 80
Enemy
Attack: 12
Defense: 5
Health: 100
And it tells you nothing.  It doesn't tell you if the enemy has a Poison skill that chunks a set amount of your health or a percentage of max health.  It doesn't tell you if the enemy has no defense against Fire element skills/equipment.
I can and have created enemies with much lower stats and health pools than the players are expected to have, but are as dangerous as a mid-dungeon boss in most "on the market" RPG's.  It's all a matter of how you program the combat, your encounters, and your skills.
Now, if you're only trying to ask, "what's a good way to present stats that anyone would understand at a glance", then most RPG's actually have this covered.  Even if they only use images of swords and shields and staves.
It's really only when you get into like a dozen or more stats that the UI becomes a problem as it will have a lack of "explanation of what this does" to the player.  Many of your "Tactical RPG's" have this problem (like Final Fantasy Tactics and games like it).
Even my own game attempts to avoid this issue of "don't know what that stat does" with two of its own:  Speed and Reflex.  I had to rename "Agility" to "Dexterity" and then I renamed "Dexterity" to "Speed" just to make the relationship between "Speed" and "Reflex" more apparent (Speed being a stat you attack with, and Reflex being a stat you defend against Speed with).  It's success rate for intuition among the low amount of test players I've got is/was about 78%.  But... that data is limited and biased and not useful to extrapolate from.
Still, the wording the dev uses, or the images they use to tell you what means what, and then the ability to "intuit" what those things do either through gameplay or the meaning of the word is what is heavily relied upon.
comradecid said:
- if stats such as INT, DEF, DEX, DEM, ABC, XYZ, etc. were indicated using indecipherable symbols instead of text/acronyms, how might a player come to understand each stat's role, utility, and potential in gameplay? could a player learn how to use this system without ever truly knowing the actual identity of its composite parts?
Click to expand...
I'm not sure why this is a question.  If the symbol is indecipherable, then the question answers itself.  A user can't decipher it by its very definition, so they can't identify it at all.  Lack of identification at any point (because it's indecipherable) would mean they can't understand that it is even a stat, much less what stat it is, or even what it might do.
I wonder if you perhaps meant "indistinguishable" instead?  Or maybe some form of "incongruent"/"inconsistant"?
This is sort of what I meant about "overly flowery language".  A lot of what you wrote reads like this.  The words sound "sophisticated", but are put together in such a way that they basically say nonsense or create contradictions.
comradecid said:
- if mana/magic points didn't exist, but the player could still use magic
that did not depend upon or draw from MP
... mechanically speaking, how could the player cast a spell whilst in combat? what would the player experience during gameplay? what restrictions might it entail, and what possibilities might it unlock?
Click to expand...
I'm also not sure what you're asking here.  D&D uses "spell slots" for magic.  Other games approach it differently with cooldowns.  Some have you spend reagents to cast spells (where you may use Oil to cast Fireball, Slip, or even Blind in different proportions to other ingredients).  Some treat spells the same as if you were using a Potion in combat (and so you must buy the spell to use it).
An easy example of reagent use is "Secret of Evermore" for the SNES.  An easy example of "use the spell like an item" would be Final Fantasy 8 for the Playstation.
Spell Slots I haven't seen used for a while, so I'm unfamiliar if that's in any modern games.  Cooldowns for spell usage instead of MP is fairly common, even in MMO's, so you should probably have already played at least one of those in recent years if you game at all.
I, personally, just have the 1 example of "spell that costs no MP", and that's just... a baseline magic skill all my Mages can use in combat when they have no MP to draw from.  It allows them to remain 100% viable in combat even when they can't cast their big spells.  They've always got their "basic attack" spell that will deal magic damage to enemies.
comradecid said:
- if experience points/levels didn't exist, how would you indicate/demonstrate to the player their 'progress' and level of personal development? what is 'experience'? if it played an active mechanical part of an overall system, what would that be?
Click to expand...
Do you mean in the abstract or real?  In a video game, "experience" is just the explanation given to indicate a player "is more skilled" in combat.  It's a "gamey" system so that it makes sense, especially since you can't really translate things like "muscle memory" and "technique" into a stat block to run damage calculations with.
Effectively, it's just "short hand" for "now your character is skilled enough to handle tougher threats".
If you're asking what happens if you eliminate level ups and XP from a game...  Eh, I've done it.  Two separate systems so far.
Second Shoreline handles XP and Levels as "a means to unlocking new content", it doesn't give you stats or anything.  That content is largely shortcuts around the map and new quests (the completion of Quests is what gives you stat points to allocate), but can also include new shops that open and other stuff.  It's used as a means to "promote exploration", rather than "grind for power".  Progression is then the tangible completion of quests and the gaining of stats (or finding equipment).  "Personal Development" of characters is handled mostly through storytelling.
"Tempest" (working title) handles XP and levels as "Renown" and "Favor".  You gain and spend "Favor" for services in town (the town has no money or use for it, so you are essentially using goodwill to acquire things like training and new equipment).  If you kill 5 slimes, you might accrue 10 Favor that you could spend on 1 "Wooden Sword", or even "Basic Training", which will burn 24 hours of your clock, but raise you 1 point of "Attack".  When you accrue enough "Favor", you earn "Renown".  Each higher point of Renown unlocks new services in town or even new questlines as you are "more well known for helping the community".  This system does favor some grinding, but the limiting factor is always going to be the "time spent" mechanic.  The game takes place over the course of 20 years, and though 24 hours for training seems "a drop in the bucket", it can quickly add up, especially as older forms of training lock off and newer ones take much longer.  Each "quest to kill some slimes" could also burn a few hours of your day, or a whole day, or a week if you're really unlucky.  Managing your time is pretty important to the game as the world WILL progress without you.
Hopefully that answers your question.

I've heard necromancy is allowed on this subforum, so here's my pet peeve that wasn't mentioned yet: incomplete effect descriptions.
For example, in
Metaphor: ReFantazio
, the protagonist's ultimate skill claims to deal "extreme physical Almighty damage", but in reality, it scales off whichever stat is higher between Strength and Magic.
Another example: the recent
Pokémon
games. One Ability, Water Bubble, has the following description:
Lowers the power of Fire-type moves done to the Pokémon and prevents the Pokémon from getting a burn.
Click to expand...
The Ability does that... as well as
doubling the power of this Pokémon's Water-type moves
. This completely hidden effect is the best aspect of the Pokémon with this Ability, Dewpider/Araquanid, as well as the fact they were overlooked by player at first.
Now, I get it: this skill and this Ability aren't the simplest effects in any JRPG. But even on more basic spells and states, it can be hard to grasp, say, the difference between "heavy" and "severe" damage, and that's assuming all "severe" damage skills don't have different base damage.

posts.author: 3rr0r1n5ynt4x
posts.body:
There are 2 things I absolutely despise:
- Unclear or vague tool tips. I want details and they should be reliable. If I have a e.g. a skill called Fireball I don't want to read "Inflicts fire damage" or even worse "Inflicts some damage". A good description would be something like
"Inflicts 70-120 fire damage to the target and to each opponent 1 square next to it. Has a 25% chance to inflict [BURN] for 4 turns.
[BURN]: Inflicts 1% MaxHP Damage every turn."
- Using symbols instead of text and not having an explanation to those symbols close by. To take the example from before:
This is bad:
- "Inflicts 70-120  damage to the target and to each opponent 1 square next to it. Has a 25% chance to inflict ️." If this is only about elemental types I can let it slide, maybe it's ok to replace fire, wind, earth etc. with fitting symbols (although honestly, most games already screw that up because there is no clear symbol for e.g. earth damage. Bonus points if you have nature damage and earth damage in your game etc.). However, what the hell is ️supposed to mean? I mean in that case it's actually kinda clear and I can ASSUME it means burning, however, I still don't know what EXACTLY it does.
This gets even more frustrating with more obscure debuffs and mechanics, e.g. have a look at Darkest Dungeon. It's an AWESOME game, but what the hell is "<<" supposed to mean? Fun fact, it depends on the context, sometimes it means "shuffle" and sometimes it means "move" and both are kinda related as a mechanic but not the same. Some other ability inflicts [Debuff-Symbol]. Ok, WHAT DOES THAT MEAN?
Yes, I know I can look all of that stuff up ingame, navigate through menus, click on the enemy on the touch screen or navigate there with the analog stick, check the debuff there through 3 different screens that open up, but thats simply not cool and not necessary. Just give me a reminder of what that ability does.
Again, Darkest Dungeon is just an example, it's really a great game and there are many others out there that do it far worse.

The problem is that in most RPG's or games, those stats "are never fully explained" to anyone, so almost all players are conditioned "big stat is better" and don't look deeper into it.
Which often means you need someone to datamine the game to figure out what does what... or someone to waste a bunch of their time experimenting to figure out the exact meaning.
The reason it's "information overload" is because all the stats and formulas are already "hidden" from the player.  But, the more stats and such you have, the more they are likely to interact with other stats and make the game even more complicated without datamining or extensive experimentation.
Some people are into that.
I'm not.  It falls under "guide dang it!" to me.  And, my stance on that is "If your game needs a guide to be open or referenced to be played, you've done a VERY BAD job as a dev and should probably not have your job anymore".

Speaking of LUK, it's a little annoying how RPGs don't always describe what the different stats do.
For example, does DEX affect accuracy and/or evasion? Or just the damage of my ranged attacks?
Does AGI only affect my turn order? Or does it also affect my escape rate?
Does MAG affect the power of healing spells? How about my mana points?
Does VIT affect my hit points?
And then there's LUK. What does this stat do? Critical chance? Critical damage? Status effect accuracy? Status effect evasion? Just plain evasion? Drop rate? None of these things? Who knows! Forget RNGsus, this is the most important lottery in any RPG with this stat!
In other words, tooltips are cool, and every RPG needs them.
